anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, datatypes, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of optimizer choices.
Buffer Cache and Latch Contention Anomaly: Excessive serialization on hot buffer-cache pages and their latches or pins, causing sessions to stall or spin while competing for page access and flush slots.

When these two root causes coexist, queries are not only forced into full-table scans, non-covering index probes, or hot-page insert patterns by poor schema/index design, but they must also fight for the same overcrowded buffer pages, latches, and I/O slots. Observable symptoms therefore include: 1) widespread full-object or non-selective index scans that inflate buffer churn, 2) surging buffer-busy/latch wait events concentrated on a few root or data pages, 3) CPU spikes from spin-locks coupled with high I/O service times, 4) erratic query latency where some executions stall far longer than optimizer estimates, and 5) write throughput collapses during bulk loads or hot-spot inserts despite otherwise adequate hardware resources.

Causally, the sub-optimal physical design creates access patterns (e.g., range scans on unpartitioned, unindexed columns, monotonic inserts into a single data or index page, or repeated lookups requiring back-to-table fetches) that funnel many concurrent sessions toward the same limited set of buffer pages. This concentrates reads, updates, and dirty-page flushes on those pages, inflating latch acquisition and buffer pin times. In turn, the resulting latch contention prolongs page residency, reduces effective cache capacity, and magnifies the penalty of the original design flaws—encouraging yet more full scans and page churn. The feedback loop between design-induced hot spots and low-level buffer contention can degrade both transactional and analytical workloads, making the underlying issues harder to diagnose because symptoms appear both at the execution-plan level and deep inside the storage engine’s synchronization layer.

entry.official_definition: The time limit for regular expression matching operations performed by the regular expression engine.
entry.trigger_condition: A regular expression match operation exceeds regexp_time_limit.
entry.workload_impact: The regular expression operation is constrained by the configured time limit.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL server system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when statement execution exceeds a configured execution-time budget because the operation runs too long or the workload is blocked behind other work.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect query shape, access path quality, resource contention, and whether the timeout threshold should be reviewed together with the workload pattern.
